intro.html: You met the everyday words for praise and blame in earlier topics (commend, laud, rebuke, berate). These ten are rarer and stronger, the kind you find in reviews, speeches and history books.

High praise (nouns): encomium, panegyric, plaudit, paean. Harsh blame (verbs): excoriate, castigate, upbraid, lambaste. Attacking a person’s name: vilify (paint as evil), impugn (question their honesty).
A handy pattern: the four praise words are all nouns (you give a panegyric), and the six blame words are all verbs (you castigate someone).

words.def: a speech or piece of writing full of high praise
words.ex: The retiring coach received an {encomium} from every player on the team.
words.ctx: Far from the lukewarm review she expected, the critic wrote an {encomium}, calling her first novel the most beautiful book of the year.
words.etym: From Greek enkomion, a song of praise.

mn.cue: en-COME-ium: PRAISE as she COMES IN
mn.text: When Zoe comes in through the village gate with the spelling trophy, the whole town greets her with a song of high praise; that welcome is an {encomium}.

labels.text: en-COME-ium: PRAISE as she COMES IN

scene.alt: A girl walks in with a trophy under a banner as townspeople cheer her.

words.def: a public speech or piece of writing of great praise
words.ex: The principal’s {panegyric} for the retiring janitor brought the whole school to its feet.
words.ctx: The biography reads less like history than a {panegyric}: it praises every decision its subject ever made and leaves out all of his mistakes.
words.etym: From Greek panegyrikos, “for a festival of all the people,” from panegyris (a public gathering): pan- (all) + agyris (assembly).

mn.cue: PAN = ALL: praise in front of ALL
mn.text: At the school assembly, in front of everyone, the principal praises Mr. Marcus for forty years of fixing, sweeping and smiling; her speech is a {panegyric}.

scene.alt: A principal at a podium praises the shy, smiling school janitor in front of everyone.

words.def: an expression of praise or approval (usually in the plural)
words.ex: The young violinist won {plaudits} from critics across the country.
words.ctx: The new bridge earned {plaudits} from engineers and artists alike, who praised both its strength and the graceful curve of its arch.
words.etym: From Latin plaudite, “applaud!”, the word actors called out at the end of a play.
words.note: Usually used in the plural, plaudits. Applaud comes from the same root.

mn.text: When Lila finishes her violin solo, the whole hall leaps up to applaud it; the cheers and praise she wins are {plaudits}.

scene.alt: A girl bows with her violin as the audience applauds.

words.def: a song, speech or piece of writing full of joyful praise
words.ex: The film is a {paean} to small-town life.
words.ctx: After the long, dark winter, the first warm day inspired a {paean} from Grandpa, who stood on the porch and sang the praises of every crocus in the yard.
words.etym: From Greek paian, a song of thanksgiving or triumph.
words.note: Paean is said PEE-un, just like peon, but the two words have nothing in common.

mn.text: On the first warm day of spring, Grandpa Gus sits at the piano and sings a joyful song praising the sun, the robins and every new flower; it is a {paean} to spring.

scene.alt: A grandfather plays the piano and sings joyfully about spring flowers.

words.ex: The review {excoriated} the restaurant for its cold soup and rude service.
words.ctx: The coach did not simply point out the players’ mistakes; she {excoriated} them, listing every missed pass in a voice that carried across the whole field.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Latin excoriare, “to strip off the hide”: ex- (off) + corium (hide, leather).

mn.cue: EX-CORI: criticism that STINGS to the core
mn.text: The food critic tastes one spoonful of the chef’s soup and tears into it so harshly that the chef shrinks behind his ladle; she {excoriates} it.

scene.alt: A furious food critic shouts harsh words about a soup while the chef hides his face.

words.ex: The teacher {castigated} the class for leaving the art room a mess.
words.ctx: The editor {castigated} the reporter in front of the whole newsroom for printing the story without checking a single fact.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Latin castigare, “to correct, to punish,” from castus (pure). Chastise comes from the same root.

mn.text: The queen meets the late knight at the castle gate and scolds him so sharply that his armor rattles; she {castigates} him.

scene.alt: A queen points and scolds a nervous knight in armor at the castle gate.

words.ex: Mom {upbraided} us for tracking mud across the clean kitchen floor.
words.ctx: Instead of thanking the volunteers, the manager {upbraided} them for arriving five minutes late, and half of them never came back.

mn.text: Tugging Lila’s tangled braids up tight, Aunt Tia scolds, “Do you EVER brush?” She {upbraids} her.

scene.alt: An aunt scolds a girl with tangled braids who sits looking unhappy.

words.ex: Critics {lambasted} the movie for its silly plot and wooden acting.
words.ctx: Fans who had waited years for the new game {lambasted} it online, complaining that it crashed constantly and ended after just two hours.

mn.text: At the barnyard talent show, the lamb boos the rooster’s song so loudly that the rooster hides behind the hay; the lamb {lambastes} the act.

scene.alt: At a barnyard talent show, a lamb loudly boos while the rooster hides.

words.def: to speak about someone as if they were evil
words.ex: Old stories often {vilify} wolves, but real wolves rarely bother people.
words.ctx: Instead of answering the new coach’s ideas, a few angry parents tried to {vilify} her, calling her selfish and dishonest without offering a shred of proof.
words.etym: From Late Latin vilificare, “to make worthless,” from vilis (cheap, worthless).

mn.cue: VILE-ify: paint someone as a VILLAIN
mn.text: Rex hangs a poster calling the new kid a lunch-stealing villain, though it is not true at all; he is trying to {vilify} him.

labels.text: VILE-ify: paint them as a VILLAIN

scene.alt: A sneaky teen points to a sign falsely calling another boy a villain, while the boy looks hurt.

words.def: to question someone’s honesty or the truth of a claim
words.ex: The visiting coach {impugned} the referee’s fairness.
words.ctx: Rather than argue with the scientist’s findings, the critic tried to {impugn} her motives, suggesting she had faked the results to win a prize.
words.etym: From Latin impugnare, “to fight against, to attack”: in- (against) + pugnare (to fight).
words.note: Impugn attacks someone’s honesty or a claim’s truth; it does not mean to punish.

mn.cue: im-PUG-n: the PUG fights your word
mn.text: Pip says he walked the dog twice today, but the pug barks, “Did NOT!” The pug {impugns} Pip’s story.

scene.alt: A boy claims he walked the dog twice while the dog barks back that he did not.

after.cap: Rare words for praise and blame.

after.html: Impugn does not mean to punish: to impugn someone’s motives is to suggest they are dishonest. And paean is said PEE-un.

items.q: “The lawyer impugned the witness’s honesty.” The lawyer…
choices: questioned whether the witness was honest
items.why: To impugn is to attack or call into question someone’s honesty or a claim’s truth. It does not mean to punish.

items.q: Which word names a song of joyful praise?
items.why: A paean is a song or speech of praise. The others are words of blame.

items.q: Which verb means to talk about someone as if they were evil?
items.why: Vilify comes from Latin vilis, worthless: to vilify is to paint someone as vile.

items.q: Plaudit shares its root with which everyday word?
items.why: Both come from Latin plaudere, to clap.
